meta.name: SurveyBench Sample Test Set
meta.description: 5 topics with predefined quiz questions and reference survey text.

quiz.question: What are the key architectural components and design choices in large language models?
What are the major training objectives and alignment techniques used for LLMs?
How do different LLM families (GPT, LLaMA, PaLM) compare in terms of architecture and performance?
What are the key challenges in LLM deployment, including efficiency, safety, and hallucination?
What are the most promising future directions for LLM research?

topics.reference_excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing. Models such as GPT-3, PaLM, and LLaMA have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in text generation, reasoning, and few-shot learning. The transformer decoder-only architecture has become the dominant design, with scaling laws showing that performance improves predictably with model size, data size, and compute. Key training techniques include next-token prediction, RLHF for alignment, and instruction tuning. Despite their success, LLMs face challenges including hallucination, high inference cost, and safety concerns.

quiz.question: What are the fundamental architectural paradigms in graph neural networks?
What are the key theoretical results about the representational power of GNNs?
How do different GNN architectures compare in terms of expressiveness, scalability, and oversmoothing?
What are the major application domains where GNNs have achieved significant success?
What are the fundamental open problems in graph representation learning?

topics.reference_excerpt: Graph Neural Networks extend deep learning to graph-structured data. Convolutional GNNs include GCN, GraphSAGE, and GIN. Attentional models like GAT learn node weights dynamically. Message-passing frameworks provide a unified view. A key theoretical result connects GNN expressiveness to the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, with GIN achieving maximal discriminative power. GNNs face challenges including oversmoothing in deep architectures and scalability to large graphs.

quiz.question: What are the key convolutional neural network architectures that shaped modern computer vision?
How have Vision Transformers changed the paradigm of image understanding?
Compare CNNs and Vision Transformers in terms of inductive biases, data efficiency, and scalability.
What are the key tasks in computer vision beyond image classification?
How is computer vision evolving with the integration of foundation models and multimodal learning?

topics.reference_excerpt: Convolutional neural networks form the backbone of modern computer vision. Key architectures include AlexNet, VGGNet, ResNet with residual connections, and efficient models like MobileNet. Vision Transformers (ViT) have emerged as competitive alternatives, processing images as patches with self-attention. CNNs benefit from strong inductive biases like locality and translation equivariance, while ViTs offer global receptive fields. Tasks span image classification, object detection (YOLO, DETR), semantic segmentation, and image generation via diffusion models.

quiz.question: What are the fundamental approaches to collaborative filtering?
How do content-based and hybrid methods differ from pure collaborative filtering?
Compare traditional matrix factorization with neural and graph-based recommendation methods.
What are the key challenges in session-based and sequential recommendation?
How are large language models changing the landscape of recommender systems?

topics.reference_excerpt: Collaborative filtering is the most widely adopted approach in recommender systems. Matrix factorization methods like SVD and NMF decompose user-item interactions into latent factors. Neural approaches include NCF which replaces dot products with neural networks, and LightGCN which simplifies graph convolution. Session-based recommenders use RNNs and transformers for sequential prediction. Key challenges include cold-start for new users/items, position bias in implicit feedback, and data sparsity.

quiz.question: What is the standard RAG architecture and its core components?
What are the key differences between sparse retrieval (BM25) and dense retrieval methods?
Compare standard RAG with advanced variants like self-RAG, iterative RAG, and multi-hop RAG.
What are the key challenges in retrieval quality for RAG systems?
What are the most important open problems in retrieval-augmented generation?

topics.reference_excerpt: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances LLMs with external knowledge. The standard RAG pipeline includes query encoding, document retrieval from a corpus, and generation conditioned on retrieved passages. Sparse retrieval (BM25) relies on term matching while dense retrieval uses pre-trained encoders for semantic matching. Advanced variants include iterative retrieval for multi-step reasoning, self-RAG with on-demand retrieval and self-critique, and multi-hop RAG for complex queries.
